title: DVN Stock Slips Below 50-Day & 200-Day SMA: Time to Buy or Exit? - The Globe and Mail
content: Devon Energy CorporationDVN is trading below its 50-day and 200-day simple moving averages (SMAs), indicating challenges in sustaining the recent performance levels.The 50-day and 200-day SMAs are widely used technical indicators that help traders and investors identify potential support and resistance levels, as well as emerging upward or downward price trends. By smoothing out short-term price fluctuations, these indicators provide a clearer picture of a stock’s underlying momentum and long-term price direction, enabling investors to make more informed investment decisions. Devon’s earnings and cash flow remain sensitive to oil, gas and NGL prices even with hedges in place. Benchmark volatility, regional basis exposure and hedge settlements can create large swings in results and limit cash available for discretionary distributions. Yet, Devon’s decision to divest Eagle Ford converts a mature producing asset into capital for shareholder returns and balance sheet improvement.Another oil and gas company, Chevron Corporation CVX, is exploring the potential divestment of several mature oil and gas assets in the U.S. Gulf as part of its strategy to streamline operations and prioritize high-growth opportunities. CVX now wants to focus on assets that have stronger long-term growth potential.In the past six months, Devon’s shares have underperformed the Zacks Oil & Gas- Exploration and Production- United States industry’s growth. In the past six months, Chevron’s shares have gained 15.6%.Should you consider adding DVN to your portfolio only based on weakness in price movements? Let’s delve deeper and find out the factors that can help investors decide whether it is a good entry point to add DVN stock to their portfolio. Devon's expanded U.S. portfolio spans the Permian, Rockies, Anadarko and Marcellus regions, providing diversified exposure to oil, natural gas and natural gas liquids (NGLs). Higher output from newly drilled wells continues to support production growth across its operating areas, while the addition of legacy Coterra Energy assets is contributing to overall production volumes.Devon's planned divestiture of the Eagle Ford assets for $4.2 billion is expected to strengthen its financial flexibility and support shareholder returns. The company anticipates approximately $3.5 billion in proceeds after taxes and effective-date adjustments. The transaction is also expected to reduce its underlying production decline rate and corporate breakeven costs while extending its drilling inventory life, strengthening long-term operational efficiency.Devon remains focused on improving capital efficiency, reducing operating costs and realizing merger-related synergies. In its November 2026 update, the company raised its expected year-end 2026 annualized pre-tax synergy run rate to approximately $350 million from $200 million. DVN also increased its anticipated average 2027 synergies to $700 million from $600 million, reflecting progress in integrating Coterra Energy's operations and streamlining expenses.Devon ended the third quarter of 2026 with $3.4 billion in liquidity, comprising $413 million in cash and an undrawn $3 billion credit facility. Total debt stood at $10.6 billion following repayment of the remaining $750 million term loan, bringing cumulative debt reduction since the Coterra merger to $1.25 billion. With no debt maturities until the second quarter of 2027, Devon aims to reduce gross debt to approximately $9 billion in early 2027, supported by operating cash flows and anticipated Eagle Ford divestiture proceeds. This improved financial position should provide flexibility to fund development activities and shareholder distributions.Devon also employs a disciplined hedging strategy to mitigate commodity price volatility and improve cash flow visibility. As of Sept. 30, 2026, the company had hedged approximately 45% of its remaining 2026 oil production and 30% of natural gas production, providing partial protection against unfavorable price movements. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Devon’s 2026 and 2027 earnings per share is showing increases of 5.12% and 8.52%, respectively, in the past 60 days. Long-term (three to five years) earnings growth is pegged at 8%. Range ResourcesRRC operates in the same sector and has access to the Midwest, Gulf Coast, Northeast, LNG-linked markets and international NGL customers. In addition, the company has a concentrated Appalachian acreage position and a deep inventory. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Range Resources’ 2026 and 2027 earnings per share is showing increases of 3.08% and 11.46%, respectively, in the past 60 days. The return on equity (“ROE”) measures how well a company generates returns from the shareholders’ equity. ROE indicates how well management utilizes investors' funds to expand the business. Devon’s ROE has underperformed the industry average in the trailing 12 months. ROE of DVN was 14.87% compared with the industry average of 20.62%. Range Resources’ ROE is currently pegged at 19.15%, a tad lower than the industry. Devon’s shares are inexpensive on a relative basis, with its current trailing 12-month Enterprise Value/Earnings before Interest, Tax, Depreciation and Amortization (EV/EBITDA TTM) being 5.8X compared with the industry average of 9.96X. The oil and Energy business is capital-intensive and the companies operating in this industry generally borrow from the market to successfully run their operations. The current debt to capital of Devon is 20.2% compared with its industry level of 48.1%. This indicates that the company is using much less debt than its peers in the industry to successfully run operations. Devon maintains a balanced mix of oil, natural gas and NGL production, with a low-cost structure that enhances margins. Strong output from its multi-basin assets generates substantial free cash flow, helping the company strengthen the balance sheet and deliver greater shareholder value.Devon’s upward earnings estimate revisions, attractive valuation and lower leverage relative to industry peers strengthen its investment appeal. Recent share price weakness also presents a potential opportunity to acquire the stock at discounted levels.However, the company’s return on equity remains below the industry average, raising concerns about profitability. Given this weakness, investors may find it prudent to remain on the sidelines and await a more favorable entry point to add this Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) stock.You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here. Learn More Chevron Corporation (NYSE: CVX) disclosed a securities transaction involving its chief legal officer in late November. The disposal related to common shares held through an employee savings investment plan, rather than a sale identified solely as a reduction of a directly held position. The ownership disclosure separately identifies several forms of ownership, helping clarify the nature of the specific interest affected by the transaction. The energy company's latest quarterly results provide a distinct backdrop. Chevron operates across the production and processing of hydrocarbons, with business performance influenced by commodity prices, operational reliability and capital expenditure. The recent quarterly report highlighted developments in domestic production and refining activity. Those business factors have different implications for shareholders from the personal ownership transaction, which should be interpreted within the specific employee savings arrangement recorded in the disclosure. The reported disposal was dated 23 November 2026 and was executed through multiple trades. The ownership disclosure used an average price to represent those executions and identified the securities as common stock. Importantly, the affected interest was described as an indirect holding through Chevron's employee savings investment plan. A position through such a plan is distinct from common shares held directly in an individual's own account, even when both represent interests in the same issuer. Employee savings arrangements can provide participants with investment choices under the rules of the relevant plan. Where company shares form part of a participant's holdings, changes to that position can result in a reportable disposal of securities. The disclosure establishes that securities were sold from this particular arrangement and that a balance remained afterwards. It does not establish the participant's investment objectives or the reasons for changing the composition of the savings plan assets. The ownership report also records other holdings separately, including a direct common stock position and interests attributed through other arrangements. Those categories are important because they should not be treated as a single directly held account. The reporting scope reflects the applicable rules governing beneficial ownership and the nature of the individual interests. The sale is therefore best understood as a defined change in the plan-related position rather than evidence of a complete withdrawal from ownership of the company's securities. Chevron's integrated business combines activities related to producing oil and natural gas with businesses involved in processing and marketing petroleum products. Upstream operations are concerned with extracting and developing hydrocarbon resources. Downstream operations include refining crude oil into products that can be sold to customers. These activities participate in different parts of the energy value chain and can experience different commercial conditions during the same reporting period. For the upstream business, the realised value of production is influenced by the prices received for oil and gas, the mix of hydrocarbons produced and the expenses incurred in bringing those resources to market. Production volume also affects the amount of saleable output generated from the company's assets. However, higher production does not guarantee an equivalent increase in earnings because the price environment and operating costs can change independently of the quantities produced. In downstream operations, the relationship between the cost of purchasing crude and the prices obtainable for refined products is a central feature of the business. Refineries also require energy, maintenance and operating resources to transform crude into marketable products. An integrated structure provides exposure to both production and processing, but does not eliminate the commercial risks of either activity. The financial contribution from each part of the company depends on its own operating conditions and the wider energy markets. Chevron's September-quarter update identified US production growth compared with the equivalent period two years earlier. This observation describes a change over a longer interval than a single quarterly comparison. Understanding the time basis is important in an energy business, where asset additions, drilling schedules and natural changes in output from existing wells may affect production across different reporting periods. A consistent comparison helps distinguish broader production developments from temporary changes in operating activity. The company also highlighted efforts to improve the competitiveness of its Bakken business. The commercial performance of an upstream asset depends on the relationship between recoverable resources, the expense of developing them and the value of the resulting production. Competitiveness can therefore involve decisions about infrastructure, operating efficiency and capital deployment. The ultimate financial contribution depends on the operating outcomes achieved, rather than the announcement of an initiative by itself. Developments in Venezuela formed another part of the company's upstream update, including expanded acreage. Acreage represents interests associated with an area in which exploration or development activities may be undertaken under the relevant arrangements. An expanded acreage position does not immediately establish additional commercial production. The timing and economics of developing resources depend on factors such as contractual arrangements, available infrastructure, investment decisions and the regulatory setting in which the assets are operated. The company recorded record crude throughput at its US refineries in the September quarter. Throughput measures the crude oil processed by a refinery network during a specified period, making it a useful operational measure of how extensively the facilities are being used. Higher throughput can provide opportunities to produce more refined products from existing infrastructure. The contribution to profitability, however, depends on the economics of processing and selling that output during the period. Refining capacity needs to be maintained through inspections, scheduled maintenance and the replacement or repair of equipment. Periods during which facilities are unavailable can reduce the amount of crude that can be processed. Reliable operations help a refinery make use of its productive capacity, although operating at elevated utilisation also requires attention to maintenance and the safety of industrial processes. The sustained financial benefit of throughput growth is therefore linked to the ability to maintain dependable operations. Product markets can move differently from crude markets because demand for transport fuels and other refined products depends on consumption patterns and economic activity. Refiners need to manage the product mix within the capabilities of their facilities and the characteristics of the crude they process. This is another reason why a record operating volume is not equivalent to a record financial result. The value of the additional processing activity depends partly on the commercial conditions prevailing at the time. Chevron's reported earnings for the September quarter were higher than in the corresponding period of the preceding year but below the immediately previous quarter. The direction of these comparisons demonstrates how the choice of reporting base affects the interpretation of performance. A company exposed to changing energy prices and a broad operating portfolio can record materially different results over consecutive quarters without an equivalent change in the scale of every asset it owns. The earnings report also presented an adjusted financial measure that removed certain specified effects from the reported result. Such presentations help distinguish particular items from the alternative measure used by management, but both perspectives remain relevant. The statutory figures include the effects recognised under applicable accounting standards. Examining the reconciliation between those presentations provides a better basis for understanding the components of the quarter than focusing exclusively on the direction of a single earnings measure. The continuing need for capital is a defining feature of an integrated energy business. Upstream development requires investment in assets that may generate production over extended periods, while refineries need expenditure to preserve the availability and performance of their facilities. The allocation of resources between these activities can influence cash generation, production capability and the financial position of the company. An executive's personal securities disposal through a savings arrangement does not establish any change in those corporate investment decisions. Chevron's latest executive ownership disclosure is notable for the form of the interest affected: common shares held indirectly through an employee savings plan. It does not describe a decision by the company to change its production strategy or its use of capital. The September-quarter results provide a separate basis for understanding the business, with higher earnings than the equivalent quarter last year and significant operational developments in domestic production and refinery throughput. The economic value of those developments depends on market conditions as well as the operating performance of the assets involved. Subsequent operating updates will help clarify how the upstream portfolio develops, including the initiatives relating to the Bakken and the expanded acreage position in Venezuela. Refining throughput, facility availability and the commercial conditions for petroleum products provide a separate set of measures for the downstream business. Changes in the relationship between capital expenditure and cash generation will also be relevant to Chevron's financial position. These company-specific operating developments offer a more substantive basis for examining the business than assumptions about the personal motivation behind a reported ownership transaction. Q: What type of ownership transaction did Chevron (NYSE: CVX) report in November? A: Chief legal officer R. Hewitt Pate disposed of common shares held indirectly through Chevron's employee savings investment plan. The transaction was dated 23 November 2026, and the disclosed position through that arrangement remained positive afterwards. Q: What is the distinction between Chevron's upstream and downstream operations? A: Chevron's upstream activities relate to developing and producing oil and gas resources, while downstream operations include refining crude and marketing petroleum products. The two businesses experience different combinations of commodity prices, operating costs and customer demand. Q: Why is refinery throughput relevant to Chevron's operating performance? A: Throughput describes how much crude oil the facilities process over a period. Chevron reported record throughput at its US refineries during the September quarter, although the financial contribution of processing also depends on product prices, crude costs and operational expenditure. Q: Which Chevron operating developments provide context for future results? A: Developments in US production, the competitiveness of the Bakken operations and the expanded Venezuelan acreage position are relevant to Chevron's upstream portfolio. Refinery performance and the associated capital requirements will also help explain the company's operating results. Meanwhile, Bernstein revised its price target on three oil majors: ExxonMobil Corp. (XOM), Chevron Corp. (CVX), and Conoco Phillips (COP) following the midterm elections. The analyst lowered the target on all three firms, saying that oil equities may struggle to appreciate. Bernstein lowered the price target on ExxonMobil to $186 from $193 and kept an ‘Outperform’ rating on the shares. The revised target implies an upside of about 9.5% from the stock’s last close. On Chevron, Bernstein cut the price target to $233 from $248 and maintained a ‘Market Perform’ rating on the shares, which suggests an upside of about 7.7%. The analyst downgraded ConocoPhillips to ‘Market Perform’ from ‘Outperform’ and slashed the price target on the company to $122, down from $129. The revised target implies a downside of nearly 13% from its last close. According to The Fly, Bernstein said that it updated its ratings and targets in the oil and gas space following the midterm elections, adding that it believes a de-escalation between the U.S. and Iran is more probable than an escalation. The analyst added that it expects oil prices to normalize. It said that it finds oil companies attractive at oil prices above $75 per barrel, but says oil equities may struggle to appreciate. The analyst also added that it is concerned about profit-taking into year-end or rotation into beaten-down sectors, and noted that it prefers gassy exploration and production companies as a result. With ImmunityBio (IBRX) shares up more than 200% this year, founder Patrick Soon-Shiong has outlined plans to unveil decades of privately funded research at NantWorks over the next 12 months, spanning cancer therapies, AI chips and satellite tech. IBRX stock tumbled 9% on Thursday to $6.07, with shares down 30% for the week and tracking their worst week in nearly two years. Soon-Shiong said on X: “I began the release of our stealth, self-funded programs at Nantworks at a speech at Stanford last night.” NantWorks brings together public and private businesses across healthcare, energy and communications. Soon-Shiong highlighted an antibody search engine he likened to Google, part of an effort to find and treat tumors more precisely. He said that the search engine will use camelid antibodies to make tumors visible on PET scans, then targeting them with radioactive isotopes. The goal is to connect cancer detection with treatment directed at the tumor. He also outlined a system that gives doctors real-time patient data to help them make timely treatment decisions. Soon-Shiong said the tech already had FDA approval, but did not name the product. Meanwhile, Soon-Shiong outlined tech to move data faster as AI systems grow. These include high-speed WiGig wireless tech and optical chips that transmit data using light. He also highlighted U.S. factories to make optical chips and chipsets that connect AI data centers. NantOptiFab is already working in this area, making chips in California that use light to carry information for AI networks, space systems and quantum technology. An SEC filing in August named Soon-Shiong as a director and showed that the company raised $20 million by selling shares to one unnamed investor. His space ambitions include chips for use in space, satellite terminals that communicate using light, and new ways to build and launch satellites. The projects also extend to energy, materials and food safety. Soon-Shiong listed batteries that work in Arctic conditions, non-toxic methods of making graphene, biodegradable alternatives to plastic made from ocean-derived materials, and machine vision to detect harmful substances in food and baby food at the point of purchase. Soon-Shiong also spotlighted a blockchain-based exchange for tokenized securities, or digital versions of stocks and other investments. He pitched it as a way to give companies and investors more control. In January, Nant Global Finance announced plans to bring stock trading, shareholder records and blockchain settlement onto one platform. Its acquisitions included Horizon Globex, which provides technology for the Upstream exchange, and BlockAgent and Equity Stock Transfer, which maintain shareholder records. The company also planned to rename Arkonis Capital, a brokerage and trading platform, NantX. At the time, completing its brokerage acquisitions still required approval from the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA). Soon-Shiong also circled back to ImmunityBio’s work on IL-15, a protein that helps activate the body’s immune defenses. Its drug Anktiva stimulates natural killer cells and T cells, which fight cancer and infections. The company is testing whether it can help patients whose immune-cell counts are too low, a condition called lymphopenia. This also includes a sepsis trial that Soon-Shiong said had been authorized. “Trials will be starting soon in USA and Europe,” he said on Wednesday. The Phase 2 study will test Anktiva in about 50 critically ill adults with sepsis and low immune-cell counts. Researchers will compare the drug plus standard care with standard care alone to see whether it reduces deaths within 28 days. “Longevity at work. Book of our patients’ stories soon,” Soon-Shiong said. The drug is already approved in the U.S. with BCG for certain bladder cancers. ImmunityBio’s approval last month expanded its use to another group of patients whose cancer had not responded to BCG. The update comes shortly after ImmunityBio’s third-quarter results, which showed that net product revenue rose 53% from a year earlier to $48.7 million. For the first nine months, it grew 92% to $143.6 million. The company also said its Quilt-2.005 trial met its main goal in a group of bladder cancer patients who had not previously received BCG. The company is on track to seek expanded FDA approval for these patients in the fourth quarter. Shares of Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) surged 17% in after-hours trading on Thursday after the company said that its key leukemia trial results are expected this month, with its CEO pointing to the treatment’s potential to become a “transformative” immunotherapy if successful. SLS stock fell nearly 5% on Thursday to $8.03, with shares on track to post their third straight weekly decline. The update is related to the Phase 3 Regal trial of Galinpepimut-S (GPS) in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The November timeline narrows Sellas’ earlier guidance for results in the fourth quarter. “In our ongoing Phase 3 REGAL trial of GPS, we are focused on completing the final analysis following the announcement of 80th event, and we expect to announce topline primary endpoint results this month,” CEO Angelos Stergiou said. “If successful, we believe GPS could be a transformative new immunotherapy for AML patients in second complete remission.” Regal is testing GPS as a maintenance treatment for AML patients who have returned to remission after treatment for a relapse. The study’s main goal is to determine whether GPS helps these patients live longer. GPS is licensed from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and targets WT1, a protein found in a range of cancers. Sellas disclosed late last month that the trial had reached its prespecified 80th death, the milestone required to begin its final analysis. This process involves finalizing and reviewing the trial database, revealing treatment assignments and analyzing the results. Beyond GPS, Sellas is advancing its second leukemia drug, Tambiciclib, or SLS009, with investors looking ahead to fresh trial results and a major medical conference presentation. The company has enrolled 40 patients in its planned 80-patient Phase 2 study in newly diagnosed AML, up from 28 disclosed in August. The study includes patients whose disease stops responding early to Azacitidine and Venetoclax, an existing drug combination. Enrollment and treatment are currently continuing, with preliminary results expected in the fourth quarter. The development comes after a completed Phase 2 study in patients whose leukemia returned or failed to respond after prior Venetoclax-based treatment. Sellas will present the findings on Dec.14 at the American Society of Hematology (ASH) meeting in New Orleans. The study enrolled 62 patients and combined SLS009 with azacitidine and venetoclax. Across all doses, 34% of the 59 patients evaluated responded to treatment. At the dose of 30 milligrams twice weekly, 54% of patients with monocytic AML, a leukemia subtype, responded, with median survival of 5.8 months. Among patients with a TP53 mutation, 57% responded, with median survival of 8.8 months. Sellas ended September with $134.7 million in cash and cash equivalents, down from $138.3 million in June. “With $134.7 million in cash and cash equivalents as of September 30, we are well positioned to further advance these programs,” Stergiou said. Third-quarter (Q3) net loss widened to $10.1 million from $6.8 million a year earlier, while loss per share narrowed to $0.05 from $0.06. Meanwhile, research and development spending rose to $7 million from $4.2 million as Sellas prepared for a potential GPS approval application after Regal’s final analysis. Additionally, Sellas is preparing to study SLS009 in pancreatic cancer patients after laboratory findings presented in September. Working with the University of Wisconsin-Madison, researchers tested SLS009 in cancer models grown from patient tissue, including one resistant to Daraxonrasib. They also tested it alongside the experimental drug ZEN3694. Sellas said that the findings support further research into overcoming treatment resistance. However, patient trials are yet to begin. title: Can Chevron Build a Lithium Business in the Smackover Formation? - TradingView
content: Chevron Corporation CVX entered the U.S. lithium sector in June 2025, when it announced two leasehold acquisitions in the Smackover Formation in Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas. The company initially put the combined position at about 125,000 net acres and later revised that figure to about 135,000 net acres. Chevron acquired the leases to find out whether it can produce lithium from salty water found deep underground. The company is pursuing lithium mainly for energy storage, including batteries used in electric vehicles and on the power grid. Chevron is assessing the underground resource, testing direct lithium extraction and designing the facilities it would need. The process separates lithium from salty water pumped to the surface, then returns the remaining water to the underground reservoir. That work draws on skills Chevron already uses in its oil and gas business, from assessing reservoirs to drilling wells and handling fluids. The company is also refining its product specifications so it can discuss with potential customers what they need and what the project might eventually be able to supply. Chevron plans to develop the acreage in phases and adjust the pace to market conditions. The company has yet to announce when commercial production might start or how much lithium it aims to produce. Oil and gas production still drives most of Chevron’s earnings, so the near-term question for investors is what the extraction tests reveal about the project’s economics. How much lithium Chevron can recover from the brine, and what it costs to recover it, will help determine whether the acreage can support a profitable business. A U.S. lithium supply chain depends on producers being able to meet battery makers’ quality standards consistently. Producing battery-grade lithium in small batches is an early step. The next test is whether that quality holds as output increases. ExxonMobil Holdings XOM holds brine rights across more than 300,000 net acres in the Smackover Formation. ExxonMobil has produced battery-grade lithium carbonate at its Texas pilot facility using brine from southern Arkansas. ExxonMobil’s preliminary agreement with LG Chem for a potential lithium supply deal is nonbinding. The company aims to produce enough lithium for about one million electric vehicles a year by the first half of the 2030s. Occidental Petroleum OXY is testing direct lithium extraction in California’s Imperial Valley through a joint venture with BHE Renewables. Occidental’s TerraLithium subsidiary and its partner produced battery-grade lithium carbonate from geothermal brine and converted lithium chloride into lithium hydroxide in separate tests. Occidental and its partner expect demonstration operations to continue through 2027 as they assess whether the process is economically viable at commercial scale.
